name: Herodotus
note:
Cicero called him the father of history. Plutarch wrote an essay called *On the Malice of Herodotus* accusing him of bias, invention and slander. Both were reacting to the same thing: he invented the practice of ASKING, and then wrote down what he was told without always believing it.

HIS METHOD IS THE ARGUMENT. He states the rule himself, in Book VII, and extends it to everything he has written: "I however am bound to report that which is reported, though I am not bound altogether to believe it; and let this saying be considered to hold good as regards every narrative in the history." So the History contains the story of the gold-digging ants, the Phoenicians who sailed round Africa and reported the sun on their right hand — which he says he does not credit and which is precisely the detail proving they did it — and the Egyptian priests' chronology, all recorded with the source named and the doubt attached. That is not credulity. It is the first working distinction between EVIDENCE and TESTIMONY.

AND HE IS FAIR TO THE ENEMY. The Persians in this book have motives, courage and grievances; Xerxes weeps at the transience of his own army. A Greek writing a generation after the invasion had every reason to write propaganda and did not.

READ HIM AGAINST LIVY, on the neighbouring shelf. Livy sets conduct on a monument to be judged and tells you what to imitate. Herodotus collects what people said and leaves the judging to you. Two founding historians, two incompatible ideas of what history is for.

ON THE TRANSLATION. Macaulay's 1890 version is close to the Greek word order and reads stiffly for it — spellings are transliterated rather than Latinised, so it is Thermopylai, Epialtes and Plataia. It is out of copyright and exact; Rawlinson and de Sélincourt read more easily and are not.

works.title: The Proem — Book I
works.source: Herodotus, *The History*, Volume 1 (Books I–IV) · trans. G. C. Macaulay · Project Gutenberg #2707 · public domain
works.note: The opening of history, in one sentence: the inquiry is published "to the end that neither the deeds of men may be forgotten by lapse of time, nor the works great and marvellous... may lose their renown; and especially that the causes may be remembered for which these waged war with one another." Then, immediately, he starts reporting what the Persians say and the Phoenicians say, and refuses to adjudicate between them.

works.title: Solon and Croesus — Book I §28–33
works.source: Herodotus, *The History*, Volume 1 (Books I–IV) · trans. G. C. Macaulay · Project Gutenberg #2707 · public domain
works.note: The most famous conversation in Greek history, and it cannot have happened — Croesus took the throne about thirty years too late. Herodotus does not care, because it is an argument rather than a report. Shown the treasuries of the richest man alive and asked who is happiest, Solon names an obscure Athenian who died well, then two brothers who died in their sleep. Solon's own shelf holds this passage too.

works.title: Thermopylai — Book VII §201–233
works.source: Herodotus, *The History*, Volume 2 (Books V–IX) · trans. G. C. Macaulay · Project Gutenberg #2456 · public domain
works.note: The whole battle: the armies in position, the four days Xerxes waited expecting them to run, the Spartan combing his hair, Epialtes selling the mountain path, and the last stand over the body of Leonidas. It ends with the inscriptions, which Herodotus quotes because he went and read them — "Stranger, report this word, we pray, to the Spartans, that lying here in this spot we remain, faithfully keeping their laws."

works.title: Salamis — Book VIII
works.source: Herodotus, *The History*, Volume 2 (Books V–IX) · trans. G. C. Macaulay · Project Gutenberg #2456 · public domain
works.note: The battle that decided the war, and the least heroic narrative on this shelf: the Greek commanders spend most of it arguing about whether to withdraw, and Themistocles, seeing his argument about to be defeated, 'secretly went forth from the assembly' and sent his children's tutor Sikinnos to tell the Persians the Greeks were about to scatter — making retreat impossible. Herodotus reports the deception in detail, admiringly, and does not pretend it was anything else. Artemisia of Halicarnassos, the only woman commanding a ship, gets the best advice in the book and is ignored.

works.title: Marathon — Book VI §94–120
works.source: Herodotus, *The History*, Volume 2 (Books V–IX) · trans. G. C. Macaulay · Project Gutenberg #2456 · public domain
works.note:
The campaign that ATTICA-MOVES.csv cites chapter by chapter — 6.97 through 6.116 — and which this library did not hold until now. Same volume as Thermopylai and Salamis on this shelf; the register was naming a text that was not aboard.

THE INTERESTING PART IS NOT THE BATTLE. Herodotus gives the fighting a few sentences and spends the chapters around it on why men did what they did. Datis anchors off Delos and will not land armed men on sacred ground. Hippias, tyrant of Athens fifty years earlier, chooses the landing beach because he knows the country — and on the way he loses a tooth in the sand and decides the omen has already been spent. The Plataians arrive in a body, the whole force of a small city. The Lacedemonians are held at home by the full moon and reach Attica three days after leaving Sparta, too late, and go out to Marathon to look at the dead.

AND HE REPORTS WHAT HE CANNOT EXPLAIN. Seven ships taken at the water's edge. A shield displayed from the mountain to the Persians already aboard, which he records, and whose sender he says he cannot name. That is the method stated in Book VII working in Book VI: report the thing reported, and attach the doubt.

works.title: The wreck at Athos — Book VI §43–45
works.source: Herodotus, *The History*, Volume 2 (Books V–IX) · trans. G. C. Macaulay · Project Gutenberg #2456 · public domain
works.note:
492 BC, and the reason the Marathon campaign took the route it took. Mardonios rounds Mount Athos and a violent north wind takes the fleet against the mountain: THREE HUNDRED SHIPS AND MORE THAN TWENTY THOUSAND MEN.

HERODOTUS ITEMISES HOW THEY DIED, which is not what a casualty figure usually gets. Some were taken by the sea monsters that fill that water. Some were dashed on the rocks. Some drowned because they did not know how to swim. Some died of the cold. He is reporting what he was told — `it is said indeed that the number was three hundred` — and the sea monsters arrive with the same phrasing as the arithmetic.

TWO YEARS LATER THE FLEET GOES THE OTHER WAY. At 6.95 the expedition starts from Samos and crosses by the Icarian Sea between the islands rather than coasting the mainland, `because, as I think, they feared more than all else the voyage round Athos`. That `as I think` is his own inference and he marks it as one. READ THIS BEFORE THE MARATHON PASSAGE: the fear the later chapter attributes to them is earned here, and the campaign's route is a decision made by a wreck.

works.title: Before Plataia — Book IX §1–27
works.source: Herodotus, *The History*, Volume 2 (Books V–IX) · trans. G. C. Macaulay · Project Gutenberg #2456 · public domain
works.note:
Mardonios takes Athens a second time and finds it empty. The Athenians have gone to Salamis again, and they send to Sparta to say that if no help comes they will find some means of safety for themselves — which is a threat, and everyone in the room knows it.

THE SPARTANS ARE KEEPING A FESTIVAL AND DELAY TEN DAYS. Then they send five thousand Spartiates in the night without telling the envoys, so that the envoys deliver an ultimatum to men who have already marched.

It ends in a quarrel about honour: the Tegeans and the Athenians argue over who has earned the left wing, and each argues it FROM HISTORY — old battles, old kings, the sons of Heracles. The Athenians win the wing by out-arguing them and then say they will stand wherever they are told.

works.title: Plataia — the ten days · Book IX §28–58
works.source: Herodotus, *The History*, Volume 2 (Books V–IX) · trans. G. C. Macaulay · Project Gutenberg #2456 · public domain
works.note:
Two armies in position and neither will begin, because the omens forbid crossing first and both diviners say the same thing. ELEVEN DAYS PASS.

What breaks it is water and food. The Persian cavalry rides down and fouls the Gargaphian spring, the supply road over Kithairon is cut, and the Greeks resolve to move in the night to ground where they can drink. THE NIGHT MOVE GOES WRONG — one commander refuses to stir, the centre goes to the wrong place, and dawn finds the line broken into three.

And a man rides into the Athenian camp in the dark. He gives his name as Alexander of Macedon, says he is a Hellene by descent, tells them Mardonios will attack at dawn, and asks that if the war goes well they remember him. Herodotus reports the whole speech.

works.title: Plataia — the battle · Book IX §59–89
works.source: Herodotus, *The History*, Volume 2 (Books V–IX) · trans. G. C. Macaulay · Project Gutenberg #2456 · public domain
works.note:
Mardonios sees the Greek line gone in the morning and takes it for flight. He crosses the Asopos and comes on shouting, in confused numbers, thinking to make short work of it.

THE SPARTANS STAND AND WILL NOT ENGAGE, because the sacrifices are against them, while men are being killed by arrows in front of Demeter's precinct. Pausanias looks to the temple of Hera and prays, and the omens change.

Mardonios is killed by Aeimnestos, a Spartan, with a stone. Artabazos, who commanded forty thousand and had argued against fighting at all, marches them away without engaging and does not stop until Thessaly. And Herodotus names the best men on both sides — the Barbarians as well — which is the habit that makes him worth reading.

works.title: Mykale — Book IX §90–105
works.source: Herodotus, *The History*, Volume 2 (Books V–IX) · trans. G. C. Macaulay · Project Gutenberg #2456 · public domain
works.note:
ON THE SAME DAY, ACROSS THE AEGEAN. Herodotus says so flatly and then reports a rumour he cannot check: that word of Plataia reached the men at Mykale before the fighting, a herald's staff lying on the beach, and the army believing it.

The Persians beach their ships at Mykale and put an enclosure round them of stones and timber, cutting down fruit-trees for it, having sent the Phoenician squadron away. The Greeks land and take it. The Ionians in the Persian line change sides during the battle, and the revolt that began Book V begins again here and this time holds.

The war that Marathon started ends in these chapters, and it ends twice in one day.

works.title: Sestos, and the end · Book IX §106–122
works.source: Herodotus, *The History*, Volume 2 (Books V–IX) · trans. G. C. Macaulay · Project Gutenberg #2456 · public domain
works.note:
The Hellenes sail to the Hellespont, find the bridges already broken by weather, and besiege Sestos through the winter until the defenders are eating boiled bed-cords.

IT TURNS ON A STORY HERODOTUS DOES NOT ENDORSE. Artaÿktes, who had stripped the shrine of Protesilaos and farmed its sacred land, is being held for ransom when a guard's salted fish leap and writhe on the fire like newly caught. Artaÿktes reads it as the god telling him what he is owed. He is nailed to boards above the shore anyway, and his son stoned in front of him. The whole tale is attributed — `it is said by the men of the Chersonese` — and left standing.

AND THEN THE LAST CHAPTER GOES BACK TO CYRUS, sixty years and a whole empire earlier. The Persians ask to leave their poor rugged country for better land, and Cyrus tells them that soft ground makes soft men and they should prepare to be subjects rather than rulers. They choose the poor land. THE HISTORY OF THE WAR ENDS ON THE DECISION THAT MADE THE EMPIRE THAT LOST IT.

works.title: Sardis, and the arrow — Book V §97–105
works.source: Herodotus, *The History*, Volume 2 (Books V–IX) · trans. G. C. Macaulay · Project Gutenberg #2456 · public domain
works.note:
WHY THERE WAS A PERSIAN FLEET IN ATTICA AT ALL. Everything else on this shelf about the war begins after the grievance; this is the grievance.

**Aristagoras**, turned away at Sparta, comes to Athens and carries the assembly — Herodotus remarks drily that it seems easier to impose upon thirty thousand than upon one man. Twenty Athenian ships go, with five Eretrian, and the Ionians take **Sardis** without resistance.

AND THEN IT BURNS BY ACCIDENT. The houses were built of reeds, and the brick ones thatched with reeds; one soldier fires one house and the city goes. The temple of the native goddess **Hybebe** goes with it — WHICH THE PERSIANS LATER GAVE AS THEIR REASON FOR BURNING TEMPLES IN GREECE, and which is the sentence standing behind Eretria at 6.101.

The Athenians go home and refuse to come back. And at 5.105 the report reaches **Darius**, who asks who the Athenians are, and having been told, ASKS FOR HIS BOW: he shoots an arrow into the sky and says `Zeus, that it may be granted me to take vengeance upon the Athenians` — then orders a servant to say to him three times at every dinner, `Master, remember the Athenians`.

THOSE ARE THE FIRST WORDS IN THE STORY. Book VI has no speech at the launching and none before the fleet sails; the campaign's one recorded utterance from the Persian side is here, at a table, six years earlier.
